caps.t:
Iwo Jima is where Marines raised the most
famous American flag of the Second World

War, and today almost nobody
is allowed to land there.

A Marine cameraman filmed
that flag going up in colour,
four days into the battle.
The fighting went on for another month,

and nearly seven thousand Americans died
taking an island of about eight square
miles.
They were sent there mainly for a runway,

halfway between America's
bomber bases and Tokyo.

So was that runway worth
seven thousand American lives?
For decades the usual answer was yes,
that it saved far more lives than it cost,

until a Marine historian went
back through the numbers.

And the reason you can't land there
now is still lying under the sand.

By the end of 1944,
America's biggest bombers,

the B-29 Superfortresses, were flying
from the Mariana Islands to bomb Japan.
It was a long round trip over open sea,

and a badly damaged plane had
nowhere to land on the way home.
Iwo Jima sat halfway along that route,
and it was in Japanese hands.

Its radar gave Japan two hours'
warning of every B-29 raid.

Fighters from the island
attacked the bombers.

They went after the crippled
ones on the way home.

In October 1944, the Joint Chiefs ordered
Admiral Chester Nimitz to take it within
three months.
The plan was to end the warnings,
give the bombers fighter escorts,

and give crippled B-29s somewhere
to land on the way home.

The Marines studied the intelligence on
the island and asked the Navy for ten days
of shelling before they landed.

The Navy said it had neither the
time nor the ammunition to spare,
and offered three.

The Marines kept pleading and
offered to settle for four,
and the answer was still three.
Bad weather cut into even those.

One Marine officer later said they'd had
about thirteen hours of fire in thirty-four
hours of daylight.

But there was a problem nobody on
the ships could see from the sea.

Most of the men they were shooting
at were already underground.

The Japanese commander was Lieutenant
General Tadamichi Kuribayashi,

who had spent several years as a young
officer at Japan's embassies in America and
Canada.

Before the battle, he wrote to his wife
that the Americans would surely invade,
and told her not to look for his return.
He didn't plan to fight on the beaches,
and he ruled out banzai charges,

the mass attacks that had thrown away
Japanese troops on other islands.

He wanted a long, slow battle of nerves
that might make the Americans lose heart.
So he moved everything underground,

the guns, the command posts, the
barracks and the aid stations.
By the time the Marines landed,

more than eleven miles of
tunnels had been finished.
One position inside Mount Suribachi,
the volcano at the island's southern tip,
went seven stories deep.

His men were told to hold their positions
and take ten American lives for every one
of theirs.

So what went wrong with the
American count of his men?
There's no fresh water on Iwo Jima,
only rain caught in tanks.

From that, the planners worked out that no
more than twelve or thirteen thousand men
could live there.

The Marines came ashore expecting
about thirteen thousand defenders,

and Kuribayashi had more
than twenty thousand,

living on half-rations
of water for months.

The Marines landed on the
morning of 19 February

1945, on three thousand
yards of black volcanic sand.

For the first hour, the beaches
were quieter than anyone had feared,
but it didn't last.

Kuribayashi waited until the beaches
were jammed with men and machines.

Shortly after ten o'clock, hundreds of
guns that had been aimed at those beaches
long before opened up.

By that night, thirty
thousand Marines were ashore,

and about one in twelve
had already been hit.

The Marines waited all night for the
banzai charge they'd met on other islands,

and it never came, that
night or any other.

And it got worse once
they moved off the beach,

because the men shooting at
them were almost never in sight.

The Americans would rarely see a live
Japanese soldier on Iwo Jima until the very
end.

Two days after the landing, kamikaze
planes sank the escort carrier Bismarck Sea
just off the island.

Inland, every cave and bunker
had to be taken one at a time,

often with flamethrowers
and tanks that fired flame.
Lieutenant Colonel Justice Chambers,
who won the Medal of Honor there,

said afterwards that each Japanese
soldier was supposed to kill ten Marines.

For a while, he said, they
were beating their quotas.
On the morning of 23 February,

a forty-man patrol under Lieutenant Harold
Schrier set off up Suribachi with a small
American flag.

A photographer from the
Marines' own magazine,

Staff Sergeant Louis
Lowery, went with them.

At twenty past ten, they tied the flag to
a length of pipe they found at the top,
and raised it.

All over the island,
men saw it and cheered.
Lowery took his pictures.

Almost at once, he was in a firefight with
a couple of Japanese soldiers who came
out of the rocks.

Hours later, a second patrol carried a
bigger flag up from a landing ship on the
beach.
An Associated Press photographer,
Joe Rosenthal, went up with them,
and so did a Marine movie cameraman,
Sergeant Bill Genaust.

Rosenthal's picture reached Guam first
and became the photograph everybody knows.

Genaust's colour film is the
one you saw at the start.

Nine days after he shot it,
Genaust was hit by enemy fire,
and his body was never recovered.

Three of the six men raising that second
flag were killed on the island too.

The flag was up on day five, and the
battle had another thirty-one days to run,

most of them in the
broken rock of the north.
On 4 March,
at the end of the second week,

a crippled B-29 called Dinah Might came
back from a raid on Tokyo and put down on
the island's main airstrip.

It was the first damaged Superfortress
to land there during the fighting,

and after a quick repair, the
Marines cheered as it took off again.

That landing was what the
island had been taken for,
and it still wasn't fully theirs.

The battle went on for
another twenty-two days,

and cost about eleven thousand
more American casualties.
At one point, a Marine officer said,

sixty thousand men were packed into less
than three and a half square miles of
broken ground.

One rifle company that landed on the first
day with a hundred and thirty-three men

in its platoons left the
island with nine of them.
On 16 March,

with nine-tenths of the
island in American hands,
Iwo Jima was declared secure.
Ten days later, before dawn on 26 March,

Japanese soldiers came out for one last
attack on the American camps near the
airfields.

Sunrise showed about three
hundred of them dead,
and more than a hundred Americans killed,
many of them pilots and Seabees.

Japanese accounts say Kuribayashi
took his own life that same night.

The Marines' landing force had more
than twenty-four thousand casualties in

thirty-six days, and more than
six thousand of them died.

Roughly one in every three Marines and
Navy corpsmen who landed was killed or

wounded, by far the highest losses in a
single battle in Marine Corps history.

With the Navy's dead at
sea and on the beaches,

the American toll comes
to nearly seven thousand.

Admiral Nimitz said that among the
Americans who served on Iwo Jima,
uncommon valor was a common virtue.

The case for paying that price
rests on the emergency landings.

The Army Air Forces' own history
says that by the end of the war,

about twenty-four hundred B-29s had
made emergency landings on the island,
carrying some twenty-five thousand airmen.

You'll often hear that every one
of those airmen was a life saved,

more than three times the Americans
who died taking the island.

General George Marshall wrote that its
airfields saved hundreds of battle-damaged
B-29s that couldn't have made it home.

In 2006, Robert Burrell, a Marine captain
who had taught history at the Naval
Academy, went through those numbers.

He argued that the sum treats
every landing as a rescue,
and the same Air Force history doesn't.

It says the island was a constant temptation
for crews in trouble to land halfway,

even when they had a reasonable
chance of making it home.

It also calls the claims of up to twenty
thousand lives saved a gross exaggeration.

Burrell counted the men
pulled out of the sea instead,

and found the rescue rate went from about
a third to about three in five once the
island was taken.
By his count, the better rescue effort,

helped by the island, saved about two
hundred and twenty more airmen than the old
rate would have.
And the fighters on the island,

he found, struggled with the
distance and the weather,

and the Air Force counted fewer than
half of their escort sorties a success.

His conclusion was that the lives saved
don't come close to the lives it cost.

So did Iwo Jima save more
Americans than it cost?

On the evidence, no, and Burrell
is right about the famous sum.

The landings were real, and some of those
crews would certainly have died in the sea
without that runway.
But by the Air Force's own account,

a lot of them would have
made it home anyway.

The island was worth having,
as a runway and a rescue base.

It just wasn't the bargain
the generals described.

The United States held the island after the
war and handed it back to Japan in 1968.

In 2007, Japan went
back to its prewar name,
Iwo To.

About a thousand Japanese civilians
had lived there before the war,
and they were all moved off in 1944.
Today it's a base for Japan's military,

and visits are limited to a few
ceremonies and memorial trips.

Once a year, American and Japanese veterans
and families meet there for a ceremony
called the Reunion of Honor.

The other reason it stays
closed is under the ground.
Kuribayashi's tunnels are still there,

and so are many of the
men who fought in them.

In March 2025, Japan's prime minister
stood on the island and said the remains of

about eleven thousand Japanese
war dead still lie there.

He promised the whole government would
work to recover them and bring them home.
Japanese search teams still go out,

and they've dug down to a cave
beneath the runway looking for them.

So it's closed because it's still
a working military airfield,

and still a grave for thousands
of the men who held it.

Our next story starts
a year after the war,

at Bikini Atoll, with the weapon
those B-29s ended it with.

The US Navy set off an atomic
bomb under its own fleet there,

and then found it
couldn't clean the ships.
